items.followUp: Differentiate between n-type and p-type semiconductors.

rubric.why: A donor impurity contributes an extra electron to the semiconductor.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a donor impurity donates an electron, usually because it is pentavalent.

rubric.why: An acceptor impurity accepts an electron, leaving a hole.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that an acceptor impurity accepts an electron, usually because it is trivalent.

modelAnswer: A donor atom is an impurity atom, usually pentavalent, that donates an extra electron to the semiconductor.
An acceptor atom is an impurity atom, usually trivalent, that accepts an electron and leaves a hole in the semiconductor.

items.followUp: Define a supersaturated solution and state how it differs from a saturated solution.

rubric.why: At a specified temperature, a saturated solution already contains as much solute as can dissolve.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a saturated solution contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve at that temperature.

rubric.why: An unsaturated solution has not reached the solubility limit and can dissolve more solute.
rubric.description: Distinguishes an unsaturated solution from a saturated one.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that an unsaturated solution can still dissolve more solute at the same temperature.

modelAnswer: A saturated solution contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve in a given amount of solvent at a specified temperature.
An unsaturated solution contains less than this maximum amount, so more solute can still dissolve at that temperature.

items.followUp: What is a suspension? Give two examples.

rubric.why: A true solution is a homogeneous mixture of solute and solvent.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing a true solution as a homogeneous mixture of solute and solvent.

rubric.description: Gives two examples of true solutions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming any two valid examples, such as salt water and sugar water.

modelAnswer: A true solution is a homogeneous mixture in which the solute is uniformly distributed in the solvent.
Examples are salt water and sugar water.

items.followUp: Define a strong electrolyte and give two examples.

rubric.why: A weak electrolyte produces ions by only partial ionization or dissociation in aqueous solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a weak electrolyte ionizes or dissociates only partially in aqueous solution.

rubric.why: Acetic acid and ammonium hydroxide are examples of weak electrolytes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming two valid weak electrolytes.

modelAnswer: A weak electrolyte ionizes only partially in aqueous solution and therefore conducts electricity weakly.
Examples are acetic acid and ammonium hydroxide.

items.followUp: Why is the third ionization energy of aluminium much greater than its second ionization energy?

rubric.why: Magnesium has two outer 3s electrons, and the first ionization removes one of them.
rubric.description: Identifies the outer electrons involved in the first ionization.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that magnesium has two outer 3s electrons and that the first ionization removes one.

rubric.why: The remaining electron is more strongly attracted to the positively charged magnesium ion, so its removal requires more energy.
rubric.description: Explains why the second ionization energy is higher.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that the remaining 3s electron is held more strongly by Mg+ and requires more energy to remove.

modelAnswer: Magnesium has two outer electrons in its 3s subshell; the first ionization removes one of them to form Mg+.
The remaining 3s electron is attracted more strongly by the positively charged magnesium ion, so more energy is required to remove it in the second ionization.
